provisions.verbatim: A contract of insurance is an agreement whereby one undertakes for a consideration to indemnify another against loss, damage or liability arising from an unknown or contingent event. A contract of suretyship shall be deemed to be an insurance contract, within the meaning of this Code, only if made by a surety who or which, as such, is doing an insurance business as hereinafter provided.
provisions.explanation: One party (the insurer) promises protection against a possible or uncertain event in exchange for consideration, usually a premium. A suretyship is treated as insurance under the Code only when it is issued by a surety engaged in insurance business.

provisions.verbatim: Any contingent or unknown event, whether past or future, which may damnify a person having an insurable interest, or create a liability against him, may be insured against, subject to the provisions of this chapter. The consent of the spouse is not necessary for the validity of an insurance policy taken out by a married person on his or her life or that of his or her children. All rights, title and interest in the policy of insurance taken out by an original owner on the life or health of the person insured shall automatically vest in the latter upon the death of the original owner, unless otherwise provided for in the policy.
provisions.explanation: An insurance policy can protect against an uncertain event that could cause a legally recognized loss or liability. A person may insure their own life or their child’s life without needing spousal consent. Unless the policy says otherwise, rights in a policy on someone’s life or health pass to that insured person when the original policy owner dies.

provisions.verbatim: A policy of insurance must specify: (a) The parties between whom the contract is made; (b) The amount to be insured except in the cases of open or running policies; (c) The premium, or if the insurance is of a character where the exact premium is only determinable upon the termination of the contract, a statement of the basis and rates upon which the final premium is to be determined; (d) The property or life insured; (e) The interest of the insured in property insured, if he is not the absolute owner thereof; (f) The risks insured against; and (g) The period during which the insurance is to continue.
provisions.explanation: Read this as the checklist of essential information that must appear in the policy. For example, the insurer, insured, coverage amount, premium, insured property/person, covered risk, and policy period should be identifiable. [Also stated in INS2 a. Content and form (Sections 50–51): Treat this as the policy checklist: parties, amount, premium/basis, property or life covered, interest in the property, covered risks, and duration. Some open or running policies do not state a fixed insured amount in the ordinary way.]

sourceRefs.section: i. Elements of a contract of insurance

provisions.verbatim: The term doing an insurance business or transacting an insurance business, within the meaning of this Code, shall include: (1) Making or proposing to make, as insurer, any insurance contract; (2) Making or proposing to make, as surety, any contract of suretyship as a vocation and not as merely incidental to any other legitimate business or activity of the surety; (3) Doing any kind of business, including a reinsurance business, specifically recognized as constituting the doing of an insurance business within the meaning of this Code; (4) Doing or proposing to do any business in substance equivalent to any of the foregoing in a manner designed to evade the provisions of this Code. In the application of the provisions of this Code, the fact that no profit is derived from the making of insurance contracts, agreements or transactions or that no separate or direct consideration is received therefor, shall not be deemed conclusive to show that the making thereof does not constitute the doing or transacting of an insurance business.
provisions.explanation: The Code looks at what a business actually does, not just its name or whether it earns a profit. A business may be conducting insurance activity if it assumes insurance risk or performs the statutory equivalents, including arrangements designed to evade regulation.

provisions.verbatim: Life insurance is insurance on human lives and insurance appertaining thereto or connected therewith. Every contract or undertaking for the payment of annuities including contracts for the payment of lump sums under a retirement program where a life insurance company manages or acts as a trustee for such retirement program shall be considered a life insurance contract for purposes of this Code.
provisions.explanation: Life insurance covers human life and related arrangements. Certain annuity and retirement-program contracts managed by a life insurer are also treated as life insurance contracts under the Code.

provisions.verbatim: An insurance upon life may be made payable on the death of the person, or on his surviving a specified period, or otherwise contingently on the continuance or cessation of life. Every contract or pledge for the payment of endowments or annuities shall be considered a life insurance contract for purposes of this Code. In the absence of a judicial guardian, the father, or in the latter’s absence or incapacity, the mother, of any minor, who is an insured or a beneficiary under a contract of life, health, or accident insurance, may exercise, in behalf of said minor, any right under the policy, without necessity of court authority or the giving of a bond, where the interest of the minor in the particular act involved does not exceed Five hundred thousand pesos (P500,000.00) or in such reasonable amount as may be determined by the Commissioner. Such right may include, but shall not be limited to, obtaining a policy loan, surrendering the policy, receiving the proceeds of the Policy, and giving the minor’s consent to any transaction on the policy. In the absence or in case of the incapacity of the father or mother, the grandparent, the eldest brother or sister at least eighteen (18) years of age, or any relative who has actual custody of the minor insured or beneficiary, shall act as a guardian without need of a court order or judicial appointment as such guardian, as long as such person is not otherwise disqualified or incapacitated. Payment made by the insurer pursuant to this section shall relieve such insurer of any liability under the contract.
provisions.explanation: A life policy may pay on death, survival to a stated date, or another life-related contingency. Section 182 also lets specified family members or custodial relatives exercise certain policy rights for a minor within the statutory conditions and monetary limit.

provisions.verbatim: The insurer in a life insurance contract shall be liable in case of suicide only when it is committed after the policy has been in force for a period of two (2) years from the date of its issue or of its last reinstatement, unless the policy provides a shorter period: Provided, however, That suicide committed in the state of insanity shall be compensable regardless of the date of commission.
provisions.explanation: The statutory rule generally requires the life policy to have been in force for two years before suicide is covered, unless the policy sets a shorter period. Suicide while the insured is legally in a state of insanity is treated separately by the statutory proviso.

provisions.verbatim: A policy of insurance upon life or health may pass by transfer, will or succession to any person, whether he has an insurable interest or not, and such person may recover upon it whatever the insured might have recovered.
provisions.explanation: A life or health policy may pass to another person by transfer, will, or succession. The transferee’s right to recover is subject to what the insured could have recovered under the policy. [Also stated in INS2 1. Ownership/transfer of life insurance (Sections 184–185; Section 233 as relevant): Life or health insurance can pass to another person by transfer, will or succession, and that person may claim what the insured could have claimed under the policy. Do not automatically apply property-insurance insurable-interest rules to the new owner of a life policy.]

sourceRefs.section: 1. Ownership/transfer of life insurance (Sections 184–185; Section 233 as relevant)

provisions.verbatim: Notice to an insurer of a transfer or bequest thereof is not necessary to preserve the validity of a policy of insurance upon life or health, unless thereby expressly required.
provisions.explanation: A transfer or bequest of a life or health policy does not need notice to the insurer to preserve validity unless the policy expressly requires notice. [Also stated in INS2 1. Ownership/transfer of life insurance (Sections 184–185; Section 233 as relevant): Notice to the insurer is not generally essential to preserve validity of a transferred or bequeathed life/health policy, unless the policy expressly requires it. Separate policy procedures may still matter for processing claims and changes.]

sourceRefs.section: 1. Ownership/transfer of life insurance (Sections 184–185; Section 233 as relevant)

provisions.verbatim: Unless the interest of a person insured is susceptible of exact pecuniary measurement, the measure of indemnity under a policy of insurance upon life or health is the sum fixed in the policy.
provisions.explanation: Life benefits are generally the agreed amount in the policy, not a calculation of the person’s economic value. This is one key way life insurance differs from property indemnity insurance.

Section 234 (described, not quoted, in the source): group life policies must contain specified provisions concerning grace periods, contestability, applications and representations, beneficiaries, coverage statements, and certain rights when a member’s coverage ends. Section 233’s individual-life nonforfeiture rules expressly do not apply to group-life or industrial-life policies.

provisions.verbatim: The term industrial life insurance as used in this Code shall mean that form of life insurance under which the premiums are payable either monthly or oftener, if the face amount of insurance provided in any policy is not more than five hundred times that of the current statutory minimum daily wage in the City of Manila, and if the words industrial policy are printed upon the policy as part of the descriptive matter. An industrial life policy shall not lapse for nonpayment of premium if such nonpayment was due to the failure of the company to send its representative or agent to the insured at the residence of the insured or at some other place indicated by him for the purpose of collecting such premium: Provided, That the provisions of this paragraph shall not apply when the premium on the policy remains unpaid for a period of three (3) months or twelve (12) weeks after the grace period has expired.
provisions.explanation: Industrial life insurance is a statutory category associated with frequent premium payments, a cap linked to the Manila minimum daily wage, and an “industrial policy” label. The second paragraph protects the insured in a particular situation where the insurer fails to send someone to collect the premium, subject to the stated time limit.

provisions.verbatim: Marine Insurance includes: (a) Insurance against loss of or damage to: (1) Vessels, craft, aircraft, vehicles, goods, freights, cargoes, merchandise, effects, disbursements, profits, moneys, securities, choses in action, instruments of debts, valuable papers, bottomry, and respondentia interests and all other kinds of property and interests therein, in respect to, appertaining to or in connection with any and all risks or perils of navigation, transit or transportation, or while being assembled, packed, crated, baled, compressed or similarly prepared for shipment or while awaiting shipment, or during any delays, storage, transhipment, or reshipment incident thereto, including war risks, marine builder’s risks, and all personal property floater risks; (2) Person or property in connection with or appertaining to a marine, inland marine, transit or transportation insurance, including liability for loss of or damage arising out of or in connection with the construction, repair, operation, maintenance or use of the subject matter of such insurance (but not including life insurance or surety bonds nor insurance against loss by reason of bodily injury to any person arising out of ownership, maintenance, or use of automobiles); (3) Precious stones, jewels, jewelry, precious metals, whether in course of transportation or otherwise; and (4) Bridges, tunnels and other instrumentalities of transportation and communication (excluding buildings, their furniture and furnishings, fixed contents and supplies held in storage); piers, wharves, docks and slips, and other aids to navigation and transportation, including dry docks and marine railways, dams and appurtenant facilities for the control of waterways.
provisions.explanation: Marine insurance is broader than a policy on a ship. It can cover cargo and other property connected with transportation, transit, shipping preparation, storage, and specified transportation-related risks.

provisions.verbatim: Marine protection and indemnity insurance, meaning insurance against, or against legal liability of the insured for loss, damage, or expense incident to ownership, operation, chartering, maintenance, use, repair, or construction of any vessel, craft or instrumentality in use of ocean or inland waterways, including liability of the insured for personal injury, illness or death or for loss of or damage to the property of another person.
provisions.explanation: Marine protection-and-indemnity insurance covers certain liabilities linked to operating or using vessels and related craft, including bodily injury and damage to someone else’s property.

provisions.verbatim: As used in this Code, the term fire insurance shall include insurance against loss by fire, lightning, windstorm, tornado or earthquake and other allied risks, when such risks are covered by extension to fire insurance policies or under separate policies.
provisions.explanation: Fire insurance can extend beyond fire itself, but the additional perils must be covered by the policy extension or a separate policy. Do not assume every fire policy automatically includes every natural disaster. [Also stated in INS2 e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance): Fire insurance can cover allied perils when the policy extends coverage to them or a separate policy does so. The label alone does not mean every peril is necessarily covered.]

sourceRefs.section: e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance)

provisions.verbatim: Casualty insurance is insurance covering loss or liability arising from accident or mishap, excluding certain types of loss which by law or custom are considered as falling exclusively within the scope of other types of insurance such as fire or marine. It includes, but is not limited to, employer’s liability insurance, motor vehicle liability insurance, plate glass insurance, burglary and theft insurance, personal accident and health insurance as written by non-life insurance companies, and other substantially similar kinds of insurance.
provisions.explanation: Casualty insurance is a broad non-life category for accidental loss or liability, including examples such as motor-vehicle liability, employer liability, burglary, and theft. The Code excludes risks treated as exclusively belonging to another class, such as fire or marine.

provisions.verbatim: A contract of suretyship is an agreement whereby a party called the surety guarantees the performance by another party called the principal or obligor of an obligation or undertaking in favor of a third party called the obligee. It includes official recognizances, stipulations, bonds or undertakings issued by any company by virtue of and under the provisions of Act No. 536, as amended by Act No. 2206.
provisions.explanation: There are three main roles: the principal/obligor must perform an obligation; the obligee is the person owed performance; and the surety guarantees performance if the principal defaults.

provisions.verbatim: The liability of the surety or sureties shall be joint and several with the obligor and shall be limited to the amount of the bond. It is determined strictly by the terms of the contract of suretyship in relation to the principal contract between the obligor and the obligee.
provisions.explanation: The obligee may enforce the surety’s liability as provided by the bond, but the amount is capped by the bond and the terms of the suretyship agreement. “Joint and several” means the surety’s liability is not merely a remote promise to pay after exhausting every remedy against the principal, subject to the contract and applicable law.

provisions.verbatim: Microinsurance is a financial product or service that meets the risk protection needs of the poor where: (a) The amount of contributions, premiums, fees or charges, computed on a daily basis, does not exceed seven and a half percent (7.5%) of the current daily minimum wage rate for nonagricultural workers in Metro Manila; and (b) The maximum sum of guaranteed benefits is not more than one thousand (1,000) times of the current daily minimum wage rate for nonagricultural workers in Metro Manila.
provisions.explanation: Microinsurance is designed to make risk protection affordable for lower-income households. The statutory definition uses premium/contribution and benefit limits tied to the current Metro Manila minimum daily wage, so the actual peso amounts can change as wage rates change.

provisions.verbatim: No insurance company or mutual benefit association shall engage in the business of microinsurance unless it possesses all the requirements as may be prescribed by the Commissioner. The Commissioner shall issue such rules and regulations governing microinsurance.
provisions.explanation: Organizations must meet the Insurance Commissioner’s requirements and regulations before offering microinsurance.

provisions.verbatim: The term bancassurance shall mean the presentation and sale to bank customers by an insurance company of its insurance products within the premises of the head office of such bank duly licensed by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas or any of its branches under such rules and regulations which the Commissioner and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas may promulgate. To engage in bancassurance arrangement, a bank is not required to have equity ownership of the insurance company. No insurance company shall enter into a bancassurance arrangement unless it possesses all the requirements as may be prescribed by the Commissioner and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. No insurance product under this section, whether life or non-life, shall be issued or delivered unless in the form previously approved by the Commissioner.
provisions.explanation: Bancassurance is insurance sold to bank customers by an insurer within bank premises under Insurance Commission and BSP regulation. The bank does not have to own part of the insurer, but the required regulatory conditions must be satisfied.

provisions.verbatim: Personnel tasked to present and sell insurance products within the bank premises shall be duly licensed by the Commissioner and shall be subject to the rules and regulations of this Act.
provisions.explanation: People presenting and selling insurance in the bank must have the appropriate license; the bank setting does not exempt the activity from insurance regulation.

provisions.verbatim: Every stipulation in a policy of insurance for the payment of loss whether the person insured has or has not any interest in the property insured, or that the policy shall be received as proof of such interest, and every policy executed by way of gaming or wagering, is void.
provisions.explanation: A policy cannot validly guarantee payment on property when the insured has no interest in it, and parties cannot use insurance as a bet. They cannot simply waive the requirement of insurable interest to make a wagering contract look like insurance.

sourceRefs.section: a. Waiver / prohibition on wagering policies (Section 25)

provisions.verbatim: Every person has an insurable interest in the life and health: (a) Of himself, of his spouse and of his children; (b) Of any person on whom he depends wholly or in part for education or support, or in whom he has a pecuniary interest; (c) Of any person under a legal obligation to him for the payment of money, or respecting property or services, of which death or illness might delay or prevent the performance; and (d) Of any person upon whose life any estate or interest vested in him depends.
provisions.explanation: A person has an insurable interest in their own life, spouse, and children, and in other people when there is a recognized support, financial, contractual, or property-related relationship of the kind listed in the statute.

provisions.verbatim: Every interest in property, whether real or personal, or any relation thereto, or liability in respect thereof, of such nature that a contemplated peril might directly damnify the insured, is an insurable interest.
provisions.explanation: Ownership is not the only possible basis. A person can have an insurable interest when damage or destruction of the property would directly cause that person a loss.

provisions.verbatim: An insurable interest in property may consist in: (a) An existing interest; (b) An inchoate interest founded on an existing interest; or (c) An expectancy, coupled with an existing interest in that out of which the expectancy arises.
provisions.explanation: The interest may be current, developing out of an existing legal interest, or an expected benefit attached to an already existing interest. A mere hope with no underlying right is not enough.

provisions.verbatim: A carrier or depository of any kind has an insurable interest in a thing held by him as such, to the extent of his liability but not to exceed the value thereof.
provisions.explanation: A carrier or warehouse/depository may insure goods it holds, but only to the extent that it could be liable for them and never beyond the goods’ value.

provisions.verbatim: A mere contingent or expectant interest in any thing, not founded on an actual right to the thing, nor upon any valid contract for it, is not insurable.
provisions.explanation: A bare possibility of receiving something later does not create an insurable interest unless there is an existing right or a valid contract supporting the expectation.

provisions.verbatim: The measure of an insurable interest in property is the extent to which the insured might be damnified by loss or injury thereof.
provisions.explanation: The amount of insurable interest is measured by how much the insured could actually lose if the property is damaged or destroyed.

provisions.verbatim: No contract or policy of insurance on property shall be enforceable except for the benefit of some person having an insurable interest in the property insured.
provisions.explanation: A property policy must benefit someone who has a legitimate insurable interest. Otherwise, the policy is not enforceable for that property interest.

provisions.verbatim: An interest in property insured must exist when the insurance takes effect, and when the loss occurs, but need not exist in the meantime; and interest in the life or health of a person insured must exist when the insurance takes effect, but need not exist thereafter or when the loss occurs.
provisions.explanation: For property insurance, the insurable interest must exist both when coverage begins and when the loss happens, though it may not need to exist continuously between those times. For life/health insurance, it must exist when the policy takes effect, but not necessarily when the insured later dies or becomes ill.

provisions.verbatim: Except in the cases specified in the next four sections, and in the cases of life, accident, and health insurance, a change of interest in any part of a thing insured unaccompanied by a corresponding change of interest in the insurance, suspends the insurance to an equivalent extent, until the interest in the thing and the interest in the insurance are vested in the same person.
provisions.explanation: For most property policies, if the property interest changes hands but the policy interest does not change along with it, coverage may be suspended to the corresponding extent until the interests line up. The Code provides exceptions in Sections 21–24 and for life, accident, and health insurance.

provisions.verbatim: A change of interest in a thing insured, after the occurrence of an injury which results in a loss, does not affect the right of the insured to indemnity for the loss.
provisions.explanation: Once the covered loss has already happened, a later transfer of interest does not take away the insured’s right to claim for that loss.

provisions.verbatim: A change of interest in one or more of several distinct things, separately insured by one policy, does not avoid the insurance as to the others.
provisions.explanation: If one of several separately insured items changes ownership, that does not automatically invalidate coverage for the other separately insured items.

provisions.verbatim: A change of interest, by will or succession, on the death of the insured, does not avoid an insurance; and his interest in the insurance passes to the person taking his interest in the thing insured.
provisions.explanation: If the insured dies and the property passes by will or succession, the policy is not automatically avoided; the insurance interest follows the person who inherits the insured property interest.

provisions.verbatim: A transfer of interest by one of several partners, joint owners, or owners in common, who are jointly insured, to the others, does not avoid an insurance even though it has been agreed that the insurance shall cease upon an alienation of the thing insured.
provisions.explanation: When co-owners or partners are jointly insured and one transfers their share to the other insured co-owners, the policy is not automatically avoided under the rule stated here.

provisions.verbatim: A double insurance exists where the same person is insured by several insurers separately in respect to the same subject and interest.
provisions.explanation: Double insurance means the same person separately insures the same subject matter and the same interest with more than one insurer. Merely having multiple policies does not always constitute double insurance if the insured, subject, or interest differs.

provisions.verbatim: Where the insured in a policy other than life is over insured by double insurance: (a) The insured, unless the policy otherwise provides, may claim payment from the insurers in such order as he may select, up to the amount for which the insurers are severally liable under their respective contracts; (b) Where the policy under which the insured claims is a valued policy, any sum received by him under any other policy shall be deducted from the value of the policy without regard to the actual value of the subject matter insured; (c) Where the policy under which the insured claims is an unvalued policy, any sum received by him under any policy shall be deducted against the full insurable value, for any sum received by him under any policy; (d) Where the insured receives any sum in excess of the valuation in the case of valued policies, or of the insurable value in the case of unvalued policies, he must hold such sum in trust for the insurers, according to their right of contribution among themselves; (e) Each insurer is bound, as between himself and the other insurers, to contribute ratably to the loss in proportion to the amount for which he is liable under his contract.
provisions.explanation: For non-life insurance, multiple policies do not let the insured collect more than the legally recoverable value of the loss. The insured can claim from insurers subject to each policy, and insurers may have to contribute proportionately. Excess proceeds are held for the insurers rather than becoming a windfall to the insured.

provisions.verbatim: In case of an over insurance by several insurers other than life, the insured is entitled to a ratable return of the premium, proportioned to the amount by which the aggregate sum insured in all the policies exceeds the insurable value of the thing at risk.
provisions.explanation: If multiple non-life policies overinsure the property, the insured is entitled to a proportional refund of the premium attributable to the excess amount, under the conditions of this provision. [Also stated in INS1 e. Refund of premiums (Sections 80–83): When several non-life policies cover more than the insurable value, the excess premium can be returned proportionately. This prevents the insured from paying for a combined level of property coverage greater than the insurable value.]

provisions.verbatim: Unless the policy otherwise provides, where a mortgagor of property effects insurance in his own name providing that the loss shall be payable to the mortgagee, or assigns a policy of insurance to a mortgagee, the insurance is deemed to be upon the interest of the mortgagor, who does not cease to be a party to the original contract, and any act of his, prior to the loss, which would otherwise avoid the insurance, will have the same effect, although the property is in the hands of the mortgagee, but any act which, under the contract of insurance, is to be performed by the mortgagor, may be performed by the mortgagee therein named, with the same effect as if it had been performed by the mortgagor.
provisions.explanation: If the owner/mortgagor buys the policy and names the lender/mortgagee to receive proceeds, the policy is ordinarily still based on the mortgagor’s interest. The mortgagor remains a party, and acts that would invalidate coverage can still matter even if the mortgagee holds the property or policy.

sourceRefs.section: e. Multiple interests over the same property: mortgagor and mortgagee (Sections 8–9)

provisions.verbatim: If an insurer assents to the transfer of an insurance from a mortgagor to a mortgagee, and, at the time of his assent, imposes further obligations on the assignee, making a new contract with him, the acts of the mortgagor cannot affect the rights of said assignee.
provisions.explanation: If the insurer agrees to transfer the insurance to the mortgagee and makes a new contract imposing obligations on the mortgagee, the mortgagor’s later acts do not affect the mortgagee’s rights under that new contract.

sourceRefs.section: e. Multiple interests over the same property: mortgagor and mortgagee (Sections 8–9)

provisions.verbatim: An insurer is entitled to payment of the premium as soon as the thing insured is exposed to the peril insured against. Notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, no policy or contract of insurance issued by an insurance company is valid and binding unless and until the premium thereof has been paid, except in the case of a life or an industrial life policy whenever the grace period provision applies, or whenever under the broker and agency agreements with duly licensed intermediaries, a ninety (90)-day credit extension is given. No credit extension to a duly licensed intermediary should exceed ninety (90) days from date of issuance of the policy.
provisions.explanation: The general rule is payment first: a policy generally is not valid and binding until the premium is paid. The Code specifies exceptions, including a life/industrial-life grace period and a qualifying credit extension of no more than 90 days to a licensed intermediary under broker/agency agreements.

provisions.verbatim: Employees of the Republic of the Philippines, including its political subdivisions and instrumentalities, and government-owned or -controlled corporations, may pay their insurance premiums and loan obligations through salary deduction: Provided, That the treasurer, cashier, paymaster or official of the entity employing the government employee is authorized, notwithstanding the provisions of any existing law, rules and regulations to the contrary, to make deductions from the salary, wage or income of the latter pursuant to the agreement between the insurer and the government employee and to remit such deductions to the insurer concerned, and collect such reasonable fee for its services.
provisions.explanation: Government employees may pay premiums and policy loans through salary deductions when the required agreement and authorized remittance arrangements are in place.

provisions.verbatim: An acknowledgment in a policy or contract of insurance or the receipt of premium is conclusive evidence of its payment, so far as to make the policy binding, notwithstanding any stipulation therein that it shall not be binding until the premium is actually paid.
provisions.explanation: If the policy or premium receipt acknowledges payment, the acknowledgment is conclusive for making the policy binding under this section, even if another policy clause says it will not bind until actual payment.

provisions.verbatim: No policy of insurance other than life shall be cancelled by the insurer except upon prior notice thereof to the insured, and no notice of cancellation shall be effective unless it is based on the occurrence, after the effective date of the policy, of one or more of the following: (a) Nonpayment of premium; (b) Conviction of a crime arising out of acts increasing the hazard insured against; (c) Discovery of fraud or material misrepresentation; (d) Discovery of willful or reckless acts or omissions increasing the hazard insured against; (e) Physical changes in the property insured which result in the property becoming uninsurable; (f) Discovery of other insurance coverage that makes the total insurance in excess of the value of the property insured; or (g) A determination by the Commissioner that the continuation of the policy would violate or would place the insurer in violation of this Code.
provisions.explanation: Section 64 governs cancellation by the insurer of non-life insurance. Nonpayment is one permissible ground, but it is not the only one. Cancellation also requires prior notice and must rest on a listed ground that occurred after the policy became effective. [Also stated in INS2 f. Grounds and exercise of right of rescission (syllabus references consolidated): Section 64 identifies statutory grounds on which an insurer may cancel a non-life policy, subject to advance notice. It should not be casually described as the general rule for rescission at inception; cancellation and rescission are related but distinct concepts.]

sourceRefs.section: f. Grounds and exercise of right of rescission (syllabus references consolidated)

provisions.verbatim: All notices of cancellation mentioned in the preceding section shall be in writing, mailed or delivered to the named insured at the address shown in the policy, or to his broker provided the broker is authorized in writing by the policy owner to receive the notice of cancellation on his behalf, and shall state: (a) Which of the grounds set forth in Section 64 is relied upon; and (b) That, upon written request of the named insured, the insurer will furnish the facts on which the cancellation is based.
provisions.explanation: Section 65 is important when analyzing cancellation under Section 64: the notice must be written and identify the statutory ground, and the insured must be informed of the right to ask for the supporting facts. [Also stated in INS2 f. Grounds and exercise of right of rescission (syllabus references consolidated): A valid cancellation notice needs to be written, sent to the proper address/person, identify the statutory ground relied on, and tell the insured that they may ask in writing for the supporting facts.]

sourceRefs.section: f. Grounds and exercise of right of rescission (syllabus references consolidated)

provisions.verbatim: In case of insurance other than life, unless the insurer at least forty-five (45) days in advance of the end of the policy period mails or delivers to the named insured at the address shown in the policy notice of its intention not to renew the policy or to condition its renewal upon reduction of limits or elimination of coverages, the named insured shall be entitled to renew the policy upon payment of the premium due on the effective date of the renewal. Any policy written for a term of less than one (1) year shall be considered as if written for a term of one (1) year. Any policy written for a term longer than one (1) year or any policy with no fixed expiration date shall be considered as if written for successive policy periods or terms of one (1) year.
provisions.explanation: Section 66 concerns non-life policy renewal, not the initial premium-payment rule. Unless proper notice is sent at least 45 days before the policy period ends, the insured is entitled to renew upon payment of the renewal premium, subject to the statutory rule.

provisions.verbatim: An insurer may contract and accept payments, in addition to regular premium, for the purpose of paying future premiums on the policy or to increase the benefits thereof.
provisions.explanation: The insurer and policyholder may agree to make additional payments intended to cover future premiums or increase policy benefits, subject to the policy and applicable rules.

provisions.verbatim: The premium, or any portion thereof, which an insurance agent or insurance broker collects from an insured and which is to be paid to an insurance company because of the assumption of liability through the issuance of policies or contracts of insurance, shall be held by the agent or broker in a fiduciary capacity and shall not be misappropriated or converted to his own use or illegally withheld by the agent or broker. Any insurance company which delivers to an insurance agent or insurance broker a policy or contract of insurance shall be deemed to have authorized such agent or broker to receive on its behalf payment of any premium which is due on such policy or contract of insurance at the time of its issuance or delivery or which becomes due thereon. In order to ensure faithful performance by the insurance agent or insurance broker of these fiduciary responsibilities, the Insurance Commissioner shall prescribe the minimum terms and conditions on such matters in the standard agency or brokers agreement between the agents and/or the broker with the insurance companies.
provisions.explanation: An agent or broker who collects premiums must hold the money in trust and cannot keep or misuse it. When an insurer delivers the policy through an agent or broker, the Code treats that intermediary as authorized to receive the due premium on the insurer’s behalf, subject to the statute and regulatory framework.

provisions.verbatim: A provision specifying the options to which the policyholder is entitled to in the event of default in a premium payment after three (3) full annual premiums shall have been paid. Such option shall consist of: (1) A cash surrender value payable upon surrender of the policy which shall not be less than the reserve on the policy, the basis of which shall be indicated, for the then current policy year and any dividend additions thereto, reduced by a surrender charge which shall not be more than one-fifth (1/5) of the entire reserve or two and one-half percent (2½%) of the amount insured and any dividend additions thereto; and (2) One or more paid-up benefits on a plan or plans specified in the policy of such value as may be purchased by the cash surrender value.
provisions.explanation: After three full annual premiums have been paid, a policy must describe options in case the policyholder later defaults. The key options are cash surrender value or paid-up insurance purchased with that value, under the statutory limits and policy terms. [Also stated in INS2 1. Ownership/transfer of life insurance (Sections 184–185; Section 233 as relevant): After enough premiums have been paid, a policyholder should have specified nonforfeiture options rather than losing all accumulated value automatically. Depending on the policy, options may include cash surrender value or paid-up benefits.]

sourceRefs.section: c. Nonforfeiture options after default in life insurance (Section 233(f)–(h))
1. Ownership/transfer of life insurance (Sections 184–185; Section 233 as relevant)

provisions.verbatim: A provision that at any time after a cash surrender value is available under the policy and while the policy is in force, the company will advance, on proper assignment or pledge of the policy and on sole security thereof, a sum equal to, or at the option of the owner of the policy, less than the cash surrender value on the policy, at a specified rate of interest, not more than the maximum allowed by law, to be determined by the company from time to time, but not more often than once a year, subject to the approval of the Commissioner; and that the company will deduct from such loan value any existing indebtedness on the policy and any unpaid balance of the premium for the current policy year, and may collect interest in advance on the loan to the end of the current policy year, which provision may further provide that such loan may be deferred for not exceeding six (6) months after the application therefor is made;
provisions.explanation: Once cash surrender value exists and the policy remains in force, the policy may permit a loan secured solely by that policy, up to the available value and subject to interest, existing debt, unpaid premium, and regulatory limits. [Also stated in INS2 1. Ownership/transfer of life insurance (Sections 184–185; Section 233 as relevant): When the policy has cash surrender value and remains in force, it may allow the owner to borrow against that value. Existing policy debt and unpaid premiums can reduce the amount available.]

sourceRefs.section: c. Nonforfeiture options after default in life insurance (Section 233(f)–(h))
1. Ownership/transfer of life insurance (Sections 184–185; Section 233 as relevant)

provisions.verbatim: A table showing in figures cash surrender values and paid-up options available under the policy each year upon default in premium payments, during at least twenty (20) years of the policy beginning with the year in which the values and options first become available, together with a provision that in the event of the failure of the policyholder to elect one of the said options within the time specified in the policy, one of said options shall automatically take effect and no policyholder shall ever forfeit his right to same by reason of his failure to so elect;
provisions.explanation: The policy must show a year-by-year table of the available surrender values and paid-up options for at least 20 years from when they first become available. If the policyholder does not choose an option in time, one of the listed options automatically applies rather than all value being lost simply because no election was made. [Also stated in INS2 1. Ownership/transfer of life insurance (Sections 184–185; Section 233 as relevant): The policy must make the available default options visible. Failure to choose an option within the time allowed should not, by itself, cause the policyholder to lose all nonforfeiture rights; the contract should specify which option takes effect automatically.]

sourceRefs.section: c. Nonforfeiture options after default in life insurance (Section 233(f)–(h))
1. Ownership/transfer of life insurance (Sections 184–185; Section 233 as relevant)

provisions.verbatim: A provision that the policyholder shall be entitled to have the policy reinstated at any time within three (3) years from the date of default of premium payment unless the cash surrender value has been duly paid, or the extension period has expired, upon production of evidence of insurability satisfactory to the company and upon payment of all overdue premiums and any indebtedness to the company upon said policy, with interest rate not exceeding that which would have been applicable to said premiums and indebtedness in the policy years prior to reinstatement.
provisions.explanation: A lapsed qualifying individual life policy may be reinstated within three years from premium default, unless the stated exceptions apply. The policyholder must provide satisfactory evidence of insurability and pay overdue premiums and policy debt with the allowed interest. Reinstatement is not automatic merely because the insured asks for it. [Also stated in INS2 1. Ownership/transfer of life insurance (Sections 184–185; Section 233 as relevant): Reinstatement is not necessarily automatic. The statutory provision contemplates an application within the stated period, evidence of insurability satisfactory to the insurer, and payment of overdue premiums and policy indebtedness with permitted interest.]

sourceRefs.section: d. Reinstatement of a lapsed life policy (Section 233(j))
1. Ownership/transfer of life insurance (Sections 184–185; Section 233 as relevant)

provisions.verbatim: A person insured is entitled to a return of premium, as follows: (a) To the whole premium if no part of his interest in the thing insured be exposed to any of the perils insured against; (b) Where the insurance is made for a definite period of time and the insured surrenders his policy, to such portion of the premium as corresponds with the unexpired time, at a pro rata rate, unless a short period rate has been agreed upon and appears on the face of the policy, after deducting from the whole premium any claim for loss or damage under the policy which has previously accrued: Provided, That no holder of a life insurance policy may avail himself of the privileges of this paragraph without sufficient cause as otherwise provided by law.
provisions.explanation: A full refund may be due if the insured’s interest was never exposed to the insured risk. For a definite-term policy surrendered early, the usual principle is a proportional return for the unused period, subject to any agreed short-rate method, prior claims, and the life-policy proviso.

provisions.verbatim: If a peril insured against has existed, and the insurer has been liable for any period, however short, the insured is not entitled to return of premiums, so far as that particular risk is concerned.
provisions.explanation: If the insurer has carried the risk and been liable for any period, even a short one, the insured generally cannot get the premium for that particular risk returned under this provision.

provisions.verbatim: A person insured is entitled to a return of the premium when the contract is voidable, and subsequently annulled under the provisions of the Civil Code; or on account of the fraud or misrepresentation of the insurer, or of his agent, or on account of facts, or the existence of which the insured was ignorant of without his fault; or when by any default of the insured other than actual fraud, the insurer never incurred any liability under the policy. A person insured is not entitled to a return of premium if the policy is annulled, rescinded or if a claim is denied by reason of fraud.
provisions.explanation: The Code allows return of premium in specified cases such as certain annulments, insurer-side fraud or misrepresentation, facts unknown to the insured without fault, or a nonfraudulent default where the insurer never incurred liability. But the insured cannot use this section to recover premiums where fraud is the reason the policy is rescinded or a claim denied.

provisions.verbatim: The written instrument in which a contract of insurance is set forth, is called a policy of insurance.
provisions.explanation: The policy is the written instrument that sets out the insurance contract. Read it together with valid riders, endorsements, applicable law, and any application made part of the contract. Section 51 separately lists the information a policy must specify.

provisions.verbatim: The policy shall be in printed form which may contain blank spaces; and any word, phrase, clause, mark, sign, symbol, signature, number, or word necessary to complete the contract of insurance shall be written on the blank spaces provided therein. Any rider, clause, warranty or endorsement purporting to be part of the contract of insurance and which is pasted or attached to said policy is not binding on the insured, unless the descriptive title or name of the rider, clause, warranty or endorsement is also mentioned and written on the blank spaces provided in the policy. Unless applied for by the insured or owner, any rider, clause, warranty or endorsement issued after the original policy shall be countersigned by the insured or owner, which countersignature shall be taken as his agreement to the contents of such rider, clause, warranty or endorsement. Notwithstanding the foregoing, the policy may be in electronic form subject to the pertinent provisions of Republic Act No. 8792, otherwise known as the “Electronic Commerce Act” and to such rules and regulations as may be prescribed by the Commissioner.
provisions.explanation: An insurance policy can be printed or electronic. Attached clauses must be properly identified in the policy, and a rider added after issuance generally needs the insured’s or owner’s countersignature unless they applied for it. A hidden or improperly incorporated rider may not bind the insured.

provisions.verbatim: No policy, certificate or contract of insurance shall be issued or delivered within the Philippines unless in the form previously approved by the Commissioner, and no application form shall be used with, and no rider, clause, warranty or endorsement shall be attached to, printed or stamped upon such policy, certificate or contract unless the form of such application, rider, clause, warranty or endorsement has been approved by the Commissioner.
provisions.explanation: A rider adds, removes, or changes policy terms—for example, an exclusion or extra benefit. Two separate questions matter: was the rider form approved by the Insurance Commissioner, and was it properly incorporated into the policy under Section 50?

provisions.verbatim: Cover notes may be issued to bind insurance temporarily pending the issuance of the policy. Within sixty (60) days after issue of a cover note, a policy shall be issued in lieu thereof, including within its terms the identical insurance bound under the cover note and the premium therefor. Cover notes may be extended or renewed beyond such sixty (60) days with the written approval of the Commissioner if he determines that such extension is not contrary to and is not for the purpose of violating any provisions of this Code. The Commissioner may promulgate rules and regulations governing such extensions for the purpose of preventing such violations and may by such rules and regulations dispense with the requirement of written approval by him in the case of extension in compliance with such rules and regulations.
provisions.explanation: A cover note is temporary evidence that insurance has been bound while the formal policy is being prepared. Under the statutory text, the formal policy should be issued within 60 days. Extension past that period is controlled by the Code and Insurance Commission rules.

provisions.verbatim: A policy is either open, valued or running.
provisions.explanation: This section identifies the three traditional forms of non-life/property policy. The next sections explain how the amount or subject of insurance is handled in each.

provisions.verbatim: An open policy is one in which the value of the thing insured is not agreed upon, and the amount of the insurance merely represents the insurer’s maximum liability. The value of such thing insured shall be ascertained at the time of the loss.
provisions.explanation: The policy does not fix the agreed value of the property in advance. The actual value is determined when loss occurs, but the insurer will not pay beyond the policy limit and other applicable limits.

provisions.verbatim: A valued policy is one which expresses on its face an agreement that the thing insured shall be valued at a specific sum.
provisions.explanation: The policy states an agreed value for the insured thing. The statutory rules and policy language govern how that valuation is applied to total or partial loss; fraud and other statutory qualifications may matter.

provisions.verbatim: A running policy is one which contemplates successive insurances, and which provides that the object of the policy may be from time to time defined, especially as to the subjects of insurance, by additional statements or indorsements.
provisions.explanation: A running policy is designed for a continuing flow of changing property or shipments, with later statements or endorsements defining what is covered at different times.

provisions.verbatim: Every corporation, partnership, or association, duly authorized to transact insurance business as elsewhere provided in this Code, may be an insurer.
provisions.explanation: A person or entity cannot simply call itself an insurer; it must fall within the permitted entity forms and have the authority required by the Insurance Code.

provisions.verbatim: For purposes of this Code, the term insurer or insurance company shall include all partnerships, associations, cooperatives or corporations, including government-owned or -controlled corporations or entities, engaged as principals in the insurance business, excepting mutual benefit associations. Unless the context otherwise requires, the term shall also include professional reinsurers defined in Section 288. Domestic company shall include companies formed, organized or existing under the laws of the Philippines. Foreign company when used without limitation shall include companies formed, organized, or existing under any laws other than those of the Philippines.
provisions.explanation: This is the Code’s broader definition for its regulatory chapters. The entity must be acting as principal in the insurance business. The section also distinguishes domestic from foreign companies and specifically addresses professional reinsurers.

provisions.verbatim: Any person who for compensation solicits or obtains insurance on behalf of any insurance company or transmits for a person other than himself an application for a policy or contract of insurance to or from such company or offers or assumes to act in the negotiating of such insurance shall be an insurance agent within the intent of this section and shall thereby become liable to all the duties, requirements, liabilities and penalties to which an insurance agent is subject. An insurance agent is an independent contractor and not an employee of the company represented. “Insurance agent” includes an agency leader, agency manager, or their equivalent. Since the insurance industry is imbued with public interest, the insurance companies upon approval of the Commissioner may exercise wide latitude in supervising the activities of their insurance agents to ensure the protection of the insuring public.
provisions.explanation: An insurance agent solicits or negotiates insurance on behalf of an insurer. The Code classifies the agent as an independent contractor, though the insurer may supervise agent activities under Insurance Commission rules because insurance affects the public.

provisions.verbatim: Any person who for any compensation, commission or other thing of value acts or aids in any manner in soliciting, negotiating or procuring the making of any insurance contract or in placing risk or taking out insurance, on behalf of an insured other than himself, shall be an insurance broker within the intent of this Code, and shall thereby become liable to all the duties, requirements, liabilities and penalties to which an insurance broker is subject.
provisions.explanation: A broker assists the insured in obtaining insurance; an agent acts on behalf of the insurer. The practical roles can overlap in ordinary speech, but the Code uses distinct legal definitions. Licensing rules also apply; Section 307 is the related licensing provision.

provisions.verbatim: Anyone except a public enemy may be insured.
provisions.explanation: The provision is broad as to who may be an insured; it does not remove other requirements, such as insurable interest where the Code requires one.

provisions.verbatim: When an insurance contract is executed with an agent or trustee as the insured, the fact that his principal or beneficiary is the real party in interest may be indicated by describing the insured as agent or trustee, or by other general words in the policy.
provisions.explanation: An agent or trustee may appear in the policy, but the policy may identify the principal or beneficiary as the real party whose interest is insured.

provisions.verbatim: To render an insurance effected by one partner or part-owner, applicable to the interest of his co-partners or other part-owners, it is necessary that the terms of the policy should be such as are applicable to the joint or common interest.
provisions.explanation: One co-owner does not automatically insure every other co-owner’s interest. The wording of the policy must extend to the joint or common interest.

provisions.verbatim: When the description of the insured in a policy is so general that it may comprehend any person or any class of persons, only he who can show that it was intended to include him, can claim the benefit of the policy.
provisions.explanation: If a policy describes a broad class of possible insureds, a claimant must show they belong to the class the policy was intended to cover.

provisions.verbatim: A policy may be so framed that it will inure to the benefit of whomsoever, during the continuance of the risk, may become the owner of the interest insured.
provisions.explanation: The policy can be written to follow the insured interest to a later owner, but the policy must be framed that way. Do not assume every transfer of property automatically transfers its insurance; see Section 58.

provisions.verbatim: If the policy is participating, a provision that the company shall periodically ascertain and apportion any divisible surplus accruing on the policy under conditions specified therein.
provisions.explanation: A participating policy may entitle the policyholder to a share of divisible surplus, according to the policy conditions. This is not the same as a guaranteed fixed return.

sourceRefs.section: 1. Ownership/transfer of life insurance (Sections 184–185; Section 233 as relevant)

provisions.verbatim: The insured shall have the right to change the beneficiary he designated in the policy, unless he has expressly waived this right in said policy. Notwithstanding the foregoing, in the event the insured does not change the beneficiary during his lifetime, the designation shall be deemed irrevocable.
provisions.explanation: The Code addresses whether the insured reserved the power to change the beneficiary. When analyzing a problem, read the policy and ask whether the right to change was expressly waived and whether a change was actually made during the insured’s lifetime. The exact statutory wording should control your exam answer.

provisions.verbatim: Any person who is forbidden from receiving any donation under Article 739 cannot be named beneficiary of a life insurance policy by the person who cannot make any donation to him, according to said article.
provisions.explanation: The Civil Code imports the restrictions on certain void donations into beneficiary designation. Naming a person as beneficiary is not always valid merely because the person is named in the policy; Article 739 may disqualify the beneficiary in the specified relationships or circumstances.

sourceRefs.section: 2. Limitations under the New Civil Code

provisions.verbatim: The following donations shall be void: (1) Those made between persons who were guilty of adultery or concubinage at the time of the donation; (2) Those made between persons found guilty of the same criminal offense, in consideration thereof; (3) Those made to a public officer or his wife, descendants and ascendants, by reason of his office. In the case referred to in No. 1, the action for declaration of nullity may be brought by the spouse of the donor or donee; and the guilt of the donor and donee may be proved by preponderance of evidence in the same action.
provisions.explanation: Article 2012 means the specified donation disqualifications can also prevent someone from being named as a life-insurance beneficiary by the person who cannot lawfully donate to them. Apply the precise statutory categories and facts rather than assuming every emotionally or socially improper relationship is automatically covered.

sourceRefs.section: 2. Limitations under the New Civil Code

provisions.verbatim: The interest of a beneficiary in a life insurance policy shall be forfeited when the beneficiary is the principal, accomplice, or accessory in willfully bringing about the death of the insured. In such a case, the share forfeited shall pass on to the other beneficiaries, unless otherwise disqualified. In the absence of other beneficiaries, the proceeds shall be paid in accordance with the policy contract. If the policy contract is silent, the proceeds shall be paid to the estate of the insured.
provisions.explanation: A beneficiary cannot profit from willfully causing the insured’s death. The disqualified beneficiary loses their interest; the share goes to the other eligible beneficiaries or, if there are none, is handled under the policy and the statutory default.

provisions.verbatim: A neglect to communicate that which a party knows and ought to communicate, is called a concealment.
provisions.explanation: Concealment is withholding a fact that should be communicated in the insurance relationship. The duty normally focuses on facts material to the risk, not every fact about the applicant.

provisions.verbatim: A concealment whether intentional or unintentional entitles the injured party to rescind a contract of insurance.
provisions.explanation: Under the Code’s wording, concealment can support rescission even without a separate showing that the omission was deliberately fraudulent. The insurer must still establish a legally sufficient concealment under the circumstances.

provisions.verbatim: Each party to a contract of insurance must communicate to the other, in good faith, all facts within his knowledge which are material to the contract and as to which he makes no warranty, and which the other has not the means of ascertaining.
provisions.explanation: The disclosure duty is mutual and concerns material facts known to a party that the other cannot readily discover. This is the general disclosure rule for the parties to the insurance contract.

provisions.verbatim: An intentional and fraudulent omission, on the part of one insured, to communicate information of matters proving or tending to prove the falsity of a warranty, entitles the insurer to rescind.
provisions.explanation: This is a narrower rule dealing with information that would show a warranty to be false. It requires an intentional and fraudulent omission.

provisions.verbatim: Neither party to a contract of insurance is bound to communicate information of the matters following, except in answer to the inquiries of the other: (a) Those which the other knows; (b) Those which, in the exercise of ordinary care, the other ought to know, and of which the former has no reason to suppose him ignorant; (c) Those of which the other waives communication; (d) Those which prove or tend to prove the existence of a risk excluded by a warranty, and which are not otherwise material; and (e) Those which relate to a risk excepted from the policy and which are not otherwise material.
provisions.explanation: The law identifies categories that generally need not be volunteered unless the other party asks—for example, facts already known, facts the other should know with ordinary care, and facts whose disclosure was waived. Do not read the exceptions too broadly: a direct question can trigger a duty to answer.

provisions.verbatim: Materiality is to be determined not by the event, but solely by the probable and reasonable influence of the facts upon the party to whom the communication is due, in forming his estimate of the disadvantages of the proposed contract, or in making his inquiries.
provisions.explanation: Ask whether the fact would reasonably influence the insurer’s assessment of the risk or its decision to investigate, accept, decline, or price the policy. Whether the feared event later happened is not the test.

provisions.verbatim: Each party to a contract of insurance is bound to know all the general causes which are open to his inquiry, equally with that of the other, and which may affect the political or material perils contemplated; and all general usages of trade.
provisions.explanation: The parties are presumed to know generally discoverable causes affecting the risk and ordinary trade usages. The section distinguishes such general knowledge from particular material facts that the other party does not have means to ascertain.

provisions.verbatim: The right to information of material facts may be waived, either by the terms of insurance or by neglect to make inquiry as to such facts, where they are distinctly implied in other facts of which information is communicated.
provisions.explanation: A party may waive the right to specific information expressly or, in the circumstances described by the statute, by failing to inquire about facts already distinctly implied by information provided.

provisions.verbatim: Information of the nature or amount of the interest of one insured need not be communicated unless in answer to an inquiry, except as prescribed by Section 51.
provisions.explanation: The general rule does not require volunteering the exact nature or amount of an insured’s interest unless asked, but Section 51 still requires the policy to specify the insured’s interest where the insured is not the absolute owner.

provisions.verbatim: Neither party to a contract of insurance is bound to communicate, even upon inquiry, information of his own judgment upon the matters in question.
provisions.explanation: A party is not generally required to disclose a purely personal judgment or opinion about the matter, as distinct from material facts. A factual answer to a question must not be disguised as a mere opinion.

provisions.verbatim: A representation may be oral or written.
provisions.explanation: A representation may appear in a written application, be made orally, or be communicated in another recognized form. The legal analysis turns on what was represented and whether it was false and material.

provisions.verbatim: A representation may be made at the time of, or before, issuance of the policy.
provisions.explanation: A pre-issuance statement can be considered as part of the underwriting facts. The timing matters because it must relate to the contract being formed.

provisions.verbatim: The language of a representation is to be interpreted by the same rules as the language of contracts in general.
provisions.explanation: Interpret representations using ordinary contract-interpretation rules, including the wording and context—not an isolated phrase without context.

provisions.verbatim: A representation as to the future is to be deemed a promise, unless it appears that it was merely a statement of belief or expectation.
provisions.explanation: A statement about future conduct may operate as a promise. If it is only a statement of belief or expectation, the statute treats it differently.

provisions.verbatim: A representation cannot qualify an express provision in a contract of insurance, but it may qualify an implied warranty.
provisions.explanation: A representation does not rewrite an express policy term, although it may affect the operation of an implied warranty.

provisions.verbatim: A representation may be altered or withdrawn before the insurance is effected, but not afterwards.
provisions.explanation: An applicant can correct or withdraw a representation before insurance takes effect. After the contract is effected, the applicant cannot simply change the earlier statement unilaterally.

provisions.verbatim: A representation must be presumed to refer to the date on which the contract goes into effect.
provisions.explanation: Unless context indicates otherwise, assess the representation as referring to the date the insurance contract became effective.

provisions.verbatim: When a person insured has no personal knowledge of a fact, he may nevertheless repeat information which he has upon the subject, and which he believes to be true, with the explanation that he does so on the information of others; or he may submit the information, in its whole extent, to the insurer; and in neither case is he responsible for its truth, unless it proceeds from an agent of the insured, whose duty it is to give the information.
provisions.explanation: An applicant may honestly relay information received from others if the lack of personal knowledge and source are explained, or submit the information fully. The section has an express exception for information coming from the insured’s agent whose duty is to provide it.

provisions.verbatim: A representation is to be deemed false when the facts fail to correspond with its assertions or stipulations.
provisions.explanation: The factual statement and the actual facts do not match. This is the starting point for deciding whether the statement was false; materiality is assessed separately.

provisions.verbatim: If a representation is false in a material point, whether affirmative or promissory, the injured party is entitled to rescind the contract from the time when the representation becomes false.
provisions.explanation: A materially false statement or promise can give the injured party a right to rescind. The effect is tied to the point at which the representation becomes false.

provisions.verbatim: The materiality of a representation is determined by the same rules as the materiality of a concealment.
provisions.explanation: Use Section 31’s objective test: would the facts probably and reasonably influence the insurer’s risk assessment or further inquiries?

provisions.verbatim: The provisions of this chapter apply as well to a modification of a contract of insurance as to its original formation.
provisions.explanation: The disclosure and representation rules also matter when the existing insurance contract is modified, not only when it is first issued.

provisions.verbatim: A provision that if the age of the insured is considered in determining the premium and the benefits accruing under the policy, and the age of the insured has been misstated, the amount payable under the policy shall be such as the premium would have purchased at the correct age.
provisions.explanation: A mistaken age does not necessarily void the policy. If age affects the premium and benefit, the amount payable is adjusted to what the paid premium would have bought at the correct age.

provisions.verbatim: Whenever a right to rescind a contract of insurance is given to the insurer by any provision of this chapter, such right must be exercised previous to the commencement of an action on the contract. After a policy of life insurance made payable on the death of the insured shall have been in force during the lifetime of the insured for a period of two (2) years from the date of its issue or of its last reinstatement, the insurer cannot prove that the policy is void ab initio or is rescindable by reason of the fraudulent concealment or misrepresentation of the insured or his agent.
provisions.explanation: The section has two rules: a rescission right under the chapter must be exercised before an action on the policy begins, and after the stated two-year period during the insured’s lifetime, the insurer is barred from proving the policy void or rescindable for the specified fraudulent concealment or misrepresentation. This is not a blanket waiver of every possible policy defense.

sourceRefs.section: d. Incontestable clause in life insurance policies (Sections 48 and 233(b))

provisions.verbatim: A provision that the policy shall be incontestable after it shall have been in force during the lifetime of the insured for a period of two (2) years from its date of issue as shown in the policy, or date of approval of last reinstatement, except for nonpayment of premium and except for violation of the conditions of the policy relating to military or naval service in time of war.
provisions.explanation: The required policy clause mirrors the two-year incontestability rule and identifies statutory exceptions. For an exam, always check the applicable policy category, whether the policy was reinstated, whether two years ran during the insured’s lifetime, and the grounds actually raised.

sourceRefs.section: d. Incontestable clause in life insurance policies (Sections 48 and 233(b))

provisions.verbatim: A warranty is either expressed or implied.
provisions.explanation: A warranty is a policy-related undertaking or assurance. It may be expressly stated or implied by law.

sourceRefs.section: e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance)

provisions.verbatim: A warranty may relate to the past, the present, the future, or to any or all of these.
provisions.explanation: A warranty can deal with past/present facts or promise something about the future.

sourceRefs.section: e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance)

provisions.verbatim: No particular form of words is necessary to create a warranty.
provisions.explanation: The legal effect depends on the statement and policy context, not solely on whether the document uses the label “warranty.”

sourceRefs.section: e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance)

provisions.verbatim: Without prejudice to Section 51, every express warranty, made at or before the execution of a policy, must be contained in the policy itself, or in another instrument signed by the insured and referred to in the policy as making a part of it.
provisions.explanation: An express warranty must be properly documented: in the policy or a signed instrument referred to as part of the policy.

sourceRefs.section: e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance)

provisions.verbatim: A statement in a policy, of a matter relating to the person or thing insured, or to the risk, as fact, is an express warranty thereof.
provisions.explanation: A statement placed in the policy as a fact about the insured, property, or risk can operate as an express warranty.

sourceRefs.section: e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance)

provisions.verbatim: A statement in a policy, which imparts that it is intended to do or not to do a thing which materially affects the risk, is a warranty that such act or omission shall take place.
provisions.explanation: A policy statement about doing or avoiding an act that materially affects the risk can become a warranty about future conduct.

sourceRefs.section: e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance)

provisions.verbatim: When, before the time arrives for the performance of a warranty relating to the future, a loss insured against happens, or performance becomes unlawful at the place of the contract, or impossible, the omission to fulfill the warranty does not avoid the policy.
provisions.explanation: A future warranty is not breached merely because it was not performed when the insured loss occurred before performance was due, or performance became unlawful or impossible as described in the statute.

sourceRefs.section: e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance)

provisions.verbatim: The violation of a material warranty, or other material provision of a policy, on the part of either party thereto, entitles the other to rescind.
provisions.explanation: A material breach by either party can entitle the other to rescind, subject to other applicable statutory limitations and procedures.

sourceRefs.section: e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance)

provisions.verbatim: A policy may declare that a violation of specified provisions thereof shall avoid it, otherwise the breach of an immaterial provision does not avoid the policy.
provisions.explanation: A policy can specify that breach of particular terms avoids coverage. Without such a stipulation, breach of an immaterial term does not void the policy under this section.

sourceRefs.section: e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance)

provisions.verbatim: A breach of warranty without fraud merely exonerates an insurer from the time that it occurs, or where it is broken in its inception, prevents the policy from attaching to the risk.
provisions.explanation: A non-fraudulent breach usually affects coverage from the point of breach or prevents risk attachment if broken from the start. Assess materiality, timing, the policy wording, and other legal provisions.

sourceRefs.section: e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance)

provisions.verbatim: An alteration in the use or condition of a thing insured from that to which it is limited by the policy made without the consent of the insurer, by means within the control of the insured, and increasing the risks, entitles an insurer to rescind a contract of fire insurance.
provisions.explanation: A change controlled by the insured, inconsistent with the policy, made without insurer consent, and increasing risk may entitle the insurer to rescind a fire policy. The conditions are cumulative.

sourceRefs.section: e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance)

provisions.verbatim: An alteration in the use or condition of a thing insured from that to which it is limited by the policy, which does not increase the risk, does not affect a contract of fire insurance.
provisions.explanation: A change does not affect fire insurance under this section if it does not increase the risk.

sourceRefs.section: e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance)

provisions.verbatim: A contract of fire insurance is not affected by any act of the insured subsequent to the execution of the policy, which does not violate its provisions, even though it increases the risk and is the cause of the loss.
provisions.explanation: Even if an act after issuance increases risk and causes the loss, the fire policy is not affected under Section 172 if the act did not violate policy terms. Read this with Sections 170–171; it is not a universal rule for all kinds of insurance.

sourceRefs.section: e. Warranties (Sections 67–76; Sections 169–172 for fire insurance)

provisions.verbatim: A condition, stipulation, or agreement in any policy of insurance, limiting the time for commencing an action thereunder to a period of less than one (1) year from the time when the cause of action accrues, is void.
provisions.explanation: A policy term cannot cut the time to sue below one year from accrual. The cause-of-action date may depend on the contract, claims process, and relevant cases.
