sourceRefs.section: f. Grounds and exercise of right of rescission (syllabus references consolidated)

provisions.verbatim: No cancellation of the policy shall be valid unless written notice thereof is given to the land transportation operator or owner of the vehicle and to the Land Transportation Office at least fifteen (15) days prior to the intended effective date thereof. Upon receipt of such notice, the Land Transportation Office, unless it receives evidence of a new valid insurance or guaranty in cash or surety bond as prescribed in this chapter, or an endorsement of revival of the cancelled one, shall order the immediate confiscation of the plates of the motor vehicle covered by such cancelled policy. The same may be reissued only upon presentation of a new insurance policy or that a guaranty in cash or surety bond has been made or posted with the Commissioner and which meets the requirements of this chapter, or an endorsement or revival of the cancelled one.
provisions.explanation: This is a special rule for cancellation of compulsory motor-vehicle insurance: written notice must reach both the vehicle owner/operator and the LTO at least 15 days before cancellation becomes effective. It is not a general ground to rescind a life, fire, or other unrelated policy.

sourceRefs.section: f. Grounds and exercise of right of rescission (syllabus references consolidated)

provisions.verbatim: (a) No insurance company authorized to transact business in the Philippines shall issue, deliver, sell or use any variable contract in the Philippines, unless and until such company shall have satisfied the Commissioner that its financial and general condition and its methods of operations, including the issue and sale of variable contracts, are not and will not be hazardous to the public or to its policy and contract owners. No foreign insurance company shall be authorized to issue, deliver or sell any variable contract in the Philippines, unless it is likewise authorized to do so by the laws of its domicile. (b) The term variable contract shall mean any policy or contract on either a group or on an individual basis issued by an insurance company providing for benefits or other contractual payments or values thereunder to vary so as to reflect investment results of any segregated portfolio of investments or of a designated separate account in which amounts received in connection with such contracts shall have been placed and accounted for separately and apart from other investments and accounts. This contract may also provide benefits or values incidental thereto payable in fixed or variable amounts, or both. It shall not be deemed to be a security or securities as defined in The Securities Act, as amended, or in the Investment Company Act, as amended, nor subject to regulations under said Acts. (c) In determining the qualifications of a company requesting authority to issue, deliver, sell or use variable contracts, the Commissioner shall always consider the following: (1) The history, financial and general condition of the company: Provided, That such company, if a foreign company, must have deposited with the Commissioner for the benefit and security of its variable contract owners in the Philippines, securities satisfactory to the Commissioner consisting of bonds of the Government of the Philippines or its instrumentalities with an actual market value of Two million pesos (₱2,000,000.00); (2) The character, responsibility and fitness of the officers and directors of the company; and (3) The law and regulation under which the company is authorized in the state of domicile to issue such contracts. (d) If after notice and hearing, the Commissioner shall find that the company is qualified to issue, deliver, sell or use variable contracts in accordance with this Code and the regulations and rules issued thereunder, the corresponding order of authorization shall be issued. Any decision or order denying authority to issue, deliver, sell or use variable contracts shall clearly and distinctly state the reasons and grounds on which it is based.
provisions.explanation: A variable contract’s values reflect the investment results of a designated separate account or portfolio. An insurer must first satisfy the Insurance Commissioner about its financial condition and operations. For a foreign insurer, the Code also requires authorization under its home jurisdiction and the stated deposit safeguards.

provisions.verbatim: Any insurance company issuing variable contracts pursuant to this Code may in its discretion issue contracts providing a combination of fixed amount and variable amount of benefits and for option lump-sum payment of benefits.
provisions.explanation: A variable policy may combine a guaranteed/fixed component with an investment-linked component. Benefits may also be payable as a lump sum if the contract provides that option.

provisions.verbatim: Every variable contract form delivered or issued for delivery in the Philippines, and every certified form evidencing variable benefits issued pursuant to any such contract on a group basis, and the application, rider and endorsement forms applicable thereto and used in connection therewith, shall be subject to the prior approval of the Commissioner.
provisions.explanation: The policy form and related application/rider/endorsement forms for variable contracts require prior approval by the Insurance Commissioner.

provisions.verbatim: Illustration of benefits payable under any variable contract shall not include or involve projections of past investment experience into the future and shall conform with the rules and regulations promulgated by the Commissioner.
provisions.explanation: An insurer cannot present past investment returns as a projection of future performance. Illustrations must follow regulatory rules and must not mislead customers into treating historical returns as guaranteed.

provisions.verbatim: Variable contracts may be issued on the industrial life basis, provided that the pertinent provisions of this Code and of the rules and regulations of the Commissioner governing variable contracts are complied with in connection with such contracts.
provisions.explanation: The Code permits variable contracts in the industrial-life format, but only if the applicable statutory and Insurance Commission requirements are followed.

provisions.verbatim: In case of loss upon an insurance against fire, an insurer is exonerated, if written notice thereof be not given to him by an insured, or some person entitled to the benefit of the insurance, without unnecessary delay. For other non-life insurance, the Commissioner may specify the period for the submission of the notice of loss.
provisions.explanation: For fire insurance, written notice must be given without unnecessary delay. For other non-life lines, a period may be specified by the Commissioner. Read any additional policy notice terms together with the Code and case law.

sourceRefs.section: a. Notice and proof of loss (Sections 90–94)

provisions.verbatim: When a preliminary proof of loss is required by a policy, the insured is not bound to give such proof as would be necessary in a court of justice; but it is sufficient for him to give the best evidence which he has in his power at the time.
provisions.explanation: The preliminary claim proof is not the same as trial-level proof. The insured must provide the best evidence then reasonably available to them.

sourceRefs.section: a. Notice and proof of loss (Sections 90–94)

provisions.verbatim: All defects in a notice of loss, or in preliminary proof thereof, which the insured might remedy, and which the insurer omits to specify to him, without unnecessary delay, as grounds of objection, are waived.
provisions.explanation: If a defect could be corrected and the insurer fails to identify it promptly, the insurer may waive that objection. The insured should still respond promptly to requests and preserve evidence.

sourceRefs.section: a. Notice and proof of loss (Sections 90–94)

provisions.verbatim: Delay in the presentation to an insurer of notice or proof of loss is waived if caused by any act of him, or if he omits to take objection promptly and specifically upon that ground.
provisions.explanation: An insurer’s own conduct causing delay, or failure to object promptly and specifically to the delay, can waive the timing objection under the section.

sourceRefs.section: a. Notice and proof of loss (Sections 90–94)

provisions.verbatim: If the policy requires, by way of preliminary proof of loss, the certificate or testimony of a person other than the insured, it is sufficient for the insured to use reasonable diligence to procure it, and in case of the refusal of such person to give it, then to furnish reasonable evidence to the insurer that such refusal was not induced by any just grounds of disbelief in the facts necessary to be certified or testified.
provisions.explanation: If a policy asks for certification from a third person, the insured must use reasonable efforts to get it. If that person refuses, the insured should reasonably show that the refusal was not due to a legitimate reason to doubt the facts.

sourceRefs.section: a. Notice and proof of loss (Sections 90–94)

provisions.verbatim: (a) No insurance company doing business in the Philippines shall refuse, without just cause, to pay or settle claims arising under coverages provided by its policies, nor shall any such company engage in unfair claim settlement practices. Any of the following acts by an insurance company, if committed without just cause and performed with such frequency as to indicate a general business practice, shall constitute unfair claim settlement practices: (1) Knowingly misrepresenting to claimants pertinent facts or policy provisions relating to coverage at issue; (2) Failing to acknowledge with reasonable promptness pertinent communications with respect to claims arising under its policies; (3) Failing to adopt and implement reasonable standards for the prompt investigation of claims arising under its policies; (4) Not attempting in good faith to effectuate prompt, fair and equitable settlement of claims submitted in which liability has become reasonably clear; or (5) Compelling policyholders to institute suits to recover amounts due under its policies by offering without justifiable reason substantially less than the amounts ultimately recovered in suits brought by them. (b) Evidence as to numbers and types of valid and justifiable complaints to the Commissioner against an insurance company, and the Commissioner’s complaint experience with other insurance companies writing similar lines of insurance shall be admissible in evidence in an administrative or judicial proceeding brought under this section. (c) If it is found, after notice and an opportunity to be heard, that an insurance company has violated this section, each instance of noncompliance with paragraph (a) may be treated as a separate violation of this section and shall be considered sufficient cause for the suspension or revocation of the company’s certificate of authority.
provisions.explanation: The Code prohibits refusal to settle a covered claim without just cause and specifies unfair practices. The listed behavior becomes “unfair claim settlement practices” when done without just cause and frequently enough to indicate a general business practice—not merely because one isolated communication was imperfect.

provisions.verbatim: The proceeds of a life insurance policy shall be paid immediately upon maturity of the policy, unless such proceeds are made payable in installments or as an annuity, in which case the installments, or annuities shall be paid as they become due: Provided, however, That in the case of a policy maturing by the death of the insured, the proceeds thereof shall be paid within sixty (60) days after presentation of the claim and filing of the proof of death of the insured. Refusal or failure to pay the claim within the time prescribed herein will entitle the beneficiary to collect interest on the proceeds of the policy for the duration of the delay at the rate of twice the ceiling prescribed by the Monetary Board, unless such failure or refusal to pay is based on the ground that the claim is fraudulent. The proceeds of the policy maturing by the death of the insured payable to the beneficiary shall include the discounted value of all premiums paid in advance of their due dates, but are not due and payable at maturity.
provisions.explanation: Life-insurance proceeds are due immediately at maturity, subject to the payment structure stated in the policy. Where the policy matures by death, the statutory period is 60 days after presentation of the claim and filing of proof of death. The section provides interest for unjustified delay, subject to its fraud exception.

provisions.verbatim: The amount of any loss or damage for which an insurer may be liable, under any policy other than life insurance policy, shall be paid within thirty (30) days after proof of loss is received by the insurer and ascertainment of the loss or damage is made either by agreement between the insured and the insurer or by arbitration; but if such ascertainment is not had or made within sixty (60) days after such receipt by the insurer of the proof of loss, then the loss or damage shall be paid within ninety (90) days after such receipt. Refusal or failure to pay the loss or damage within the time prescribed herein will entitle the assured to collect interest on the proceeds of the policy for the duration of the delay at the rate of twice the ceiling prescribed by the Monetary Board, unless such failure or refusal to pay is based on the ground that the claim is fraudulent.
provisions.explanation: For non-life insurance, the usual deadline is 30 days after proof of loss and ascertainment of the amount by agreement or arbitration. If the amount is not ascertained within 60 days after proof of loss, the section sets a 90-day outer timeline measured from receipt of proof of loss. It also provides interest for delay, subject to the statutory fraud exception.

provisions.verbatim: In case of any litigation for the enforcement of any policy or contract of insurance, it shall be the duty of the Commissioner or the Court, as the case may be, to make a finding as to whether the payment of the claim of the insured has been unreasonably denied or withheld; and in the affirmative case, the insurance company shall be adjudged to pay damages which shall consist of attorney’s fees and other expenses incurred by the insured person by reason of such unreasonable denial or withholding of payment plus interest of twice the ceiling prescribed by the Monetary Board of the amount of the claim due the insured, from the date following the time prescribed in Section 248 or in Section 249, as the case may be, until the claim is fully satisfied: Provided, That failure to pay any such claim within the time prescribed in said sections shall be considered prima facie evidence of unreasonable delay in payment.
provisions.explanation: In litigation to enforce a policy, the Commissioner or court must determine whether payment was unreasonably denied or withheld. If so, the insurer may be liable for attorney’s fees, other reasonable expenses caused by the delay, and the statutory interest. Missing the payment deadlines is prima facie evidence of unreasonable delay, not necessarily the only evidence relevant to the final ruling.

provisions.verbatim: It is unlawful to: (a) Present or cause to be presented any fraudulent claim for the payment of a loss under a contract of insurance; and (b) Fraudulently prepare, make or subscribe any writing with intent to present or use the same, or to allow it to be presented in support of any such claim. Any person who violates this section shall be punished by a fine not exceeding twice the amount claimed or imprisonment of two (2) years, or both, at the discretion of the court.
provisions.explanation: Claim fraud is unlawful. It includes both presenting a fraudulent claim and preparing or signing a fraudulent document intended to support a claim. Do not confuse a claim that is honestly disputed or imperfectly documented with a knowingly fraudulent claim; the statutory elements matter.

provisions.verbatim: Any person having any claim upon the policy issued pursuant to this chapter shall, without any unnecessary delay, present to the insurance company concerned a written notice of claim setting forth the nature, extent and duration of the injuries sustained as certified by a duly licensed physician. Notice of claim must be filed within six (6) months from the date of accident, otherwise, the claim shall be deemed waived. Action or suit for recovery of damage due to loss or injury must be brought, in proper cases, with the Commissioner or the courts within one (1) year from denial of the claim, otherwise, the claimant’s right of action shall prescribe.
provisions.explanation: This is a special deadline for claims under the compulsory motor-vehicle insurance chapter: written notice within six months of the accident, then an action within one year from denial of claim. Do not automatically apply these deadlines to every ordinary life, fire, or health policy.

sourceRefs.section: c. Prescription of action and jurisdiction (Sections 63, 397, 439; Civil Code Article 1144)

provisions.verbatim: The Commissioner shall have the power to adjudicate claims and complaints involving any loss, damage or liability for which an insurer may be answerable under any kind of policy or contract of insurance, or for which such insurer may be liable under a contract of suretyship, or for which a reinsurer may be sued under any contract of reinsurance it may have entered into; or for which a mutual benefit association may be held liable under the membership certificates it has issued to its members, where the amount of any such loss, damage or liability, excluding interest, cost and attorney’s fees, being claimed or sued upon any kind of insurance, bond, reinsurance contract, or membership certificate does not exceed in any single claim Five million pesos (₱5,000,000.00). The power of the Commissioner does not cover the relationship between the insurance company and its agents/brokers but is limited to adjudicating claims and complaints filed by the insured against the insurance company. The authority to adjudicate granted to the Commissioner under this section shall be concurrent with that of the civil courts, but the filing of a complaint with the Commissioner shall preclude the civil courts from taking cognizance of a suit involving the same subject matter.
provisions.explanation: This section addresses which insurance disputes the Insurance Commissioner may adjudicate and states a ₱5 million threshold in the text of R.A. No. 10607, excluding interest, costs, and attorney’s fees. It is not itself a general deadline for filing a case. Check later laws and current Commission rules before relying on the threshold in a live dispute.

sourceRefs.section: c. Prescription of action and jurisdiction (Sections 63, 397, 439; Civil Code Article 1144)

provisions.verbatim: The following actions must be brought within ten years from the time the right of action accrues: (1) Upon a written contract; (2) Upon an obligation created by law; (3) Upon a judgment.
provisions.explanation: Article 1144 sets a general ten-year period for the listed categories, but do not automatically use it for every insurance dispute. A special provision of the Insurance Code or a valid policy limitation clause—subject to Section 63 and applicable jurisprudence—may govern. Identify exactly what action is being filed and when the cause of action accrued.

sourceRefs.section: c. Prescription of action and jurisdiction (Sections 63, 397, 439; Civil Code Article 1144)

provisions.verbatim: The creditor is not bound to accept payment or performance by a third person who has no interest in the fulfillment of the obligation, unless there is a stipulation to the contrary. Whoever pays for another may demand from the debtor what he has paid, except that if he paid without the knowledge or against the will of the debtor, he can recover only insofar as the payment has been beneficial to the debtor.
provisions.explanation: Article 1236 generally addresses when a third person can pay someone else’s debt and recover from the debtor. It is not the principal insurance-subrogation provision, but it can help distinguish ordinary reimbursement after payment from the insurer’s statutory/equitable rights after indemnifying an insured loss.

provisions.verbatim: If the plaintiff’s property has been insured, and he has received indemnity from the insurance company for the injury or loss arising out of the wrong or breach of contract complained of, the insurance company shall be subrogated to the rights of the insured against the wrongdoer or the person who has violated the contract. If the amount paid by the insurance company does not fully cover the injury or loss, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to recover the deficiency from the person causing the loss or injury.
provisions.explanation: Once the insurer indemnifies the insured for property loss caused by another’s wrong or breach, the insurer steps into the insured’s shoes to pursue the wrongdoer up to the amount paid. If the insurance payment does not cover the entire loss, the insured may pursue the remaining deficiency, subject to rules against double recovery.

cases.doctrine: A health-care agreement can be a contract of insurance when its substance is an undertaking, for consideration, to cover loss or expenses resulting from illness or hospitalization. The nature of the promise — not only the contract's label — matters.
cases.examUse: Do not automatically assume an HMO/health-care agreement falls outside insurance law because it is called a “health-care agreement.” Analyze the actual promise and the risk assumed.
cases.facts: Ernani Trinos obtained a health-care agreement from Philamcare and answered “no” to an application question asking whether he or family members had previously consulted or been treated for listed medical conditions. During the coverage period, he suffered a heart attack and was hospitalized. Philamcare denied the claim, alleging concealment of prior medical conditions. His wife paid the hospital expenses and pursued reimbursement.
cases.issue: Was the health-care agreement a contract of insurance, and could Philamcare avoid coverage based on alleged concealment?
cases.name: Philamcare Health Systems, Inc. v. Court of Appeals
cases.note: Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/50579. The Court also applied the rule that health-care contracts should be read liberally in favor of subscribers and that exclusionary language of doubtful meaning is construed strictly against the provider.
cases.ruling: The Supreme Court denied Philamcare's petition and affirmed the Court of Appeals. It treated the agreement as insurance in substance because Philamcare, for a fee, undertook to cover specified medical and hospitalization expenses upon a covered event. The application answers did not justify the denial based merely on opinion/belief-type responses, and the relevant contestability periods had passed.

cases.doctrine: A person need not always hold formal title or possession to have an insurable interest. A buyer/consignee may have one if the sale and related transaction mean the buyer would suffer loss if the goods were damaged. Under an all-risks cargo policy, proof of damage may shift the burden to the insurer to establish an exclusion.
cases.examUse: Memorize the sequence: (1) show cargo was in good condition when coverage attached; (2) show damage/loss on arrival; (3) the insurer must prove that an exclusion applies.
cases.facts: Choa Tiek Seng, the consignee/buyer of fishmeal shipped from Bangkok to Manila, insured the cargo under a marine “all risks” policy. When the cargo arrived, numerous bags were damaged and there was a shortage. The insurer refused to pay, arguing that no specific accidental cause had been proved and that the consignee lacked an insurable interest.
cases.issue: Was the cargo loss covered by the “all risks” policy, and did the consignee have an insurable interest in goods in transit?
cases.name: Filipino Merchants Insurance Co., Inc. v. Court of Appeals
cases.ruling: The Supreme Court denied the insurer's petition and affirmed the award for the insured. It explained that an “all risks” policy covers loss from an accidental cause unless the insurer proves an applicable exclusion. The insured's initial burden was to show that the cargo was in good condition when coverage attached and that it was damaged upon unloading; the insurer then had to show that an excluded peril caused the loss. The consignee had an insurable interest because the perfected sale gave him an equitable interest in the goods in transit.

sourceRefs.section: Case digest: Filipino Merchants Insurance Co., Inc. v. Court of Appeals

cases.doctrine: A material fact is judged by its probable and reasonable influence on the insurer's risk assessment. Failure to disclose recent medical consultations may be material even when the applicant believes the condition is minor; the non-medical nature of the policy makes truthful health disclosures especially important.
cases.examUse: Ask whether a reasonable insurer would probably be influenced by the fact when assessing the risk or deciding whether to inquire further — not whether the undisclosed fact caused the eventual loss.
cases.facts: Jaime Canilang applied for non-medical life insurance shortly after consulting a doctor twice. He was diagnosed with sinus tachycardia and acute bronchitis and had been prescribed medication, but his medical declaration stated that he had not received medical attention in the prior five years and had not been treated or consulted for listed conditions. He later died, and the insurer denied the beneficiary's claim because of nondisclosure.
cases.issue: Was the failure to disclose the recent medical consultations a material concealment allowing the insurer to rescind, even if the insured may have thought the ailments were minor?
cases.name: Vda. de Canilang v. Court of Appeals
cases.note: Court's key phrase: “probable and reasonable influence of the facts”. Full decision: https://lawyerly.ph/juris/view/c7a62
cases.ruling: Yes. The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision denying recovery under the policy. The undisclosed doctor visits, diagnoses, and medication were material because they could have prompted further inquiries or affected whether the insurer issued a non-medical policy or charged a higher premium. Materiality did not depend on the insured's subjective belief or on whether the concealed condition was ultimately the cause of death.

sourceRefs.section: Case digest: Vda. de Canilang v. Court of Appeals

cases.doctrine: The incontestability clause promotes stability and protects insured persons and beneficiaries from late repudiation. Insurers are expected to investigate policy issuance within the statutory period. The case involved a policy in force for more than two years before the insured died; the statutory text and the facts must be applied carefully when a question changes that timing.
cases.examUse: Section 48 gives the insurer two years, while the insured is alive, to investigate and establish the claimed defects. An insurer cannot continue collecting premiums and later deny liability through a belated challenge after the statutory period has passed.
cases.facts: Delia Sotero obtained a ₱100,000 life insurance policy issued on August 30, 1993 and named her niece, Cresencia Aban, as beneficiary. Sotero died on April 10, 1996, more than two years after issuance. After the claim, the insurer alleged that Sotero had not personally applied, was illiterate and sickly, and that Aban had effectively procured the policy and named herself beneficiary. The insurer denied the claim and later sued to annul or rescind the policy.
cases.issue: Could the insurer still contest or rescind the policy on allegations of fraud, concealment, misrepresentation, or lack of insurable interest after the policy had been in force during the insured's lifetime for more than two years?
cases.name: Manila Bankers Life Insurance Corporation v. Aban
cases.note: Court's key phrase: “After two years, the defenses of concealment or misrepresentation, no matter how patent or well-founded, will no longer lie”. Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/18/56125
cases.ruling: No. The Supreme Court denied the insurer's petition and affirmed the dismissal of its action. Section 48 gave the insurer two years, while the insured was alive, to investigate and establish the claimed defects.

questions.prompt: 1. Why does Section 51 not equal the usual doctrinal list of contract elements?
questions.answerKey: Section 51 lists required information in the written policy; the doctrinal elements are explained from the definition and general contract law.

questions.prompt: 2. What distinguishes first-party coverage from third-party liability coverage?
questions.answerKey: First-party: the insured’s own covered loss. Third-party: the insured’s covered liability to another person.

questions.prompt: 3. When must the insured have an insurable interest in property? How does this differ from life insurance?
questions.answerKey: Property: when insurance begins and when the loss occurs. Life/health: when insurance takes effect.

questions.prompt: 4. Under an all-risks marine policy, what must the insured initially prove, and what burden then shifts to the insurer?
questions.answerKey: The insured initially shows cargo was sound when coverage attached and damaged at unloading; the insurer then must prove that an exclusion applies.

questions.prompt: 5. What is the difference between double insurance and overinsurance?
questions.answerKey: Double insurance concerns the arrangement of multiple policies; overinsurance concerns coverage exceeding insurable value.

questions.prompt: 6. What are the general rule and statutory exceptions on premium payment under Section 77?
questions.answerKey: General rule: premium paid before binding, subject to exceptions including qualifying life/industrial-life grace periods and a broker/agency 90-day extension. Section 79 also gives effect to the policy or receipt’s acknowledgment of premium payment.

questions.prompt: 7. What conditions must be met to reinstate an individual life policy under Section 233(j)?
questions.answerKey: Within three years of premium default (unless the stated exception applies), satisfactory evidence of insurability, overdue premiums, policy indebtedness, and permitted interest.

questions.prompt: 8. Why may an insurer cancel a non-life policy under Section 64 but not simply cancel for any reason?
questions.answerKey: The Code lists allowable grounds and requires prior written notice with the statutory details; cancellation is not at-large discretion.

questions.prompt: 1. An applicant does not disclose two doctor consultations shortly before applying for life insurance. What sections govern disclosure, materiality, and the case most directly on point?
questions.answerKey: 1. Sections 26–31 and 36–46; materiality is tested under Section 31; Vda. de Canilang v. CA is the assigned case.

questions.prompt: 2. A rider is added after issuance without the insured’s application or countersignature. What statutory formalities should be checked?
questions.answerKey: 2. Sections 50 and 232: rider identification in the policy, countersignature if not applied for by the insured/owner, and prior Commission approval of the form.

questions.prompt: 3. A non-life insurer wants to cancel a policy because it discovers another policy that causes overinsurance. Which sections govern the ground and notice?
questions.answerKey: 3. Sections 64(f) and 65: discovered other insurance causing total insurance to exceed property value is a statutory ground, and written notice with the required statements is necessary.

questions.prompt: 4. A life policy has been in force during the insured’s lifetime for more than two years. What kind of concealment/misrepresentation defense is limited by Section 48?
questions.answerKey: 4. The statutory two-year rule in Section 48 and the required clause in Section 233(b), subject to the exact policy type and stated exceptions.

questions.prompt: 5. What is the difference between a policy’s open, valued, and running forms?
questions.answerKey: 5. Sections 59–62: open = value established at loss; valued = specific agreed value; running = successive insurance defined over time.

questions.prompt: 6. An insurer pays for property damage caused by a negligent third party. What is the basis for the insurer’s recovery from that third party?
questions.answerKey: 6. Civil Code Article 2207: subrogation after the insurer pays indemnity for the insured property loss.

questions.prompt: 7. What are the notice and action deadlines for a claim under the compulsory motor-vehicle insurance chapter?
questions.answerKey: 7. Section 397: written notice within six months from the accident; action within one year from denial of claim, otherwise the special statutory consequences apply.

flashcards.back: An agreement whereby one undertakes for a consideration to indemnify another against loss, damage or liability arising from an unknown or contingent event (Sec. 2(a)).
flashcards.front: Define a contract of insurance.

flashcards.back: Making/proposing insurance contracts as insurer; suretyship as a vocation; reinsurance and other business the Code recognizes as insurance; or doing the substance equivalent to evade the Code — even with no profit or separate consideration (Sec. 2(b)).

flashcards.back: Section 51 lists required policy contents (parties, amount, premium, property/life, interest, risks, period). The doctrinal elements are: insurable interest, risk/peril, insurer's undertaking, consideration, and meeting of minds.
flashcards.front: Contrast Section 51 with the doctrinal elements of an insurance contract.

flashcards.back: Individual: one person under a personal policy. Group: members under one master policy (certificates; Sec. 234 rules). Industrial: frequent premiums, face cap tied to the Manila minimum daily wage, “industrial policy” label (Sec. 235).
flashcards.front: Distinguish individual, group, and industrial life insurance.

flashcards.back: Marine: navigation/transit/transportation risks, cargo and related liabilities (Sec. 101). Fire: fire plus allied perils only if covered by extension or separate policy (Sec. 169). Casualty: accident/mishap loss or liability not exclusively in another class (Sec. 176).
flashcards.front: Distinguish marine, fire, and casualty insurance.

flashcards.back: Principal/obligor (must perform), obligee (owed performance), surety (guarantees performance). Liability is joint and several with the obligor, capped at the bond amount (Secs. 177–178).
flashcards.front: Name the three suretyship roles and the cap on the surety's liability.

flashcards.back: Property: when the insurance takes effect AND when the loss occurs. Life/health: when the insurance takes effect (need not exist later or at loss) (Sec. 19).
flashcards.front: When must insurable interest exist for property vs. life/health insurance?

flashcards.back: Double insurance = the arrangement (same person, same subject and interest, several insurers — Sec. 95). Overinsurance = coverage exceeding insurable value (claim limits in Sec. 96; premium return in Sec. 83).
flashcards.front: Contrast double insurance with overinsurance.

flashcards.back: (1) Cargo sound when coverage attached; (2) damaged/short at unloading; then (3) the insurer must prove an exclusion applies. The consignee's perfected sale gave an equitable insurable interest.
flashcards.front: State the all-risks cargo proof sequence from Filipino Merchants.

sourceRefs.section: Case digest: Filipino Merchants Insurance Co., Inc. v. Court of Appeals

flashcards.back: General rule: no policy is valid and binding until the premium is paid. Exceptions: life/industrial-life grace periods, and up to a 90-day credit extension to licensed intermediaries under broker/agency agreements (Sec. 77).
flashcards.front: State the Section 77 premium-payment rule and its exceptions.

flashcards.back: Cancellation (Secs. 64–65): non-life only, listed post-effective ground + prior written notice identifying the ground. Renewal (Sec. 66): without 45 days' advance notice of non-renewal/reduction, the insured may renew on paying the premium.
flashcards.front: Contrast cancellation under Sections 64–65 with renewal under Section 66.

flashcards.back: Within 3 years from premium default (unless cash value paid or extension expired): satisfactory evidence of insurability + all overdue premiums + policy indebtedness + permitted interest (Sec. 233(j)).
flashcards.front: What does reinstatement of a lapsed life policy require?

sourceRefs.section: d. Reinstatement of a lapsed life policy (Section 233(j))

flashcards.back: Open: value set at loss; policy states only maximum liability (Sec. 60). Valued: specific agreed value on the policy face (Sec. 61). Running: successive insurances defined over time by statements/endorsements (Sec. 62).
flashcards.front: Distinguish open, valued, and running policies.

flashcards.back: Three checks: (1) rider form approved by the Commissioner (Sec. 232); (2) descriptive title written on the policy's blank spaces (Sec. 50); (3) if added after issuance without the insured/owner's application, countersigned by the insured/owner (Sec. 50).
flashcards.front: What formalities make a rider bind the insured?

flashcards.back: An agent solicits or negotiates insurance on behalf of the insurer (Sec. 309; independent contractor). A broker acts on behalf of the insured in soliciting, negotiating, or procuring insurance (Sec. 310).
flashcards.front: Who does an insurance agent represent, and how does a broker differ?

flashcards.back: A beneficiary who is a principal, accomplice, or accessory in willfully causing the insured's death forfeits the interest; the share passes to the other beneficiaries (unless disqualified), else per the policy, else to the insured's estate (Sec. 12).
flashcards.front: What happens to the share of a beneficiary who willfully causes the insured's death?

flashcards.back: Written notice without unnecessary delay, given by the insured or a person entitled to benefit; otherwise the insurer is exonerated (Sec. 90). For other non-life lines, the Commissioner may specify the period.
flashcards.front: What notice does a fire-loss claim require, and what happens without it?

sourceRefs.section: a. Notice and proof of loss (Sections 90–94)

flashcards.back: Not by the event, but solely by the probable and reasonable influence of the facts on the party owed communication — in estimating the disadvantages of the proposed contract or in making inquiries (Sec. 31; Canilang).
flashcards.front: How is materiality tested for concealment and representation?

flashcards.back: After a life policy payable on death has been in force during the insured's lifetime for 2 years from issue or last reinstatement, the insurer cannot prove it void ab initio or rescindable for fraudulent concealment/misrepresentation (Sec. 48; clause required by Sec. 233(b)).
flashcards.front: State the two-year incontestability rule and its limits.

sourceRefs.section: d. Incontestable clause in life insurance policies (Sections 48 and 233(b))

flashcards.back: A policy (group or individual) whose benefits, payments, or values vary with investment results of a segregated portfolio or separate account; the insurer needs prior Commissioner authorization (Sec. 238).
flashcards.front: What is a variable contract?

flashcards.back: Life proceeds maturing by death: within 60 days after claim presentation and proof of death (Sec. 248). Non-life: within 30 days after proof of loss plus ascertainment, or within 90 days after proof of loss if unascertained within 60 days (Sec. 249). Delay earns double-ceiling interest unless the claim is fraudulent.
flashcards.front: Within what time must life and non-life proceeds be paid?
